result: The manuscript describes a theoretical model of behavioral sequences based on parallel activation and hierarchical suppression, where different movements are readied simultaneously and compete for output, with suppression determining their sequential execution order.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C6-C10 establish the theoretical framework from prior literature. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established work (Lashley, 1951; Houghton and Hartley, 1995; Bullock, 2004; Seeds et al., 2014) and represent accepted models in the field. The theoretical foundation is appropriately attributed and documented.

result: Previous work established that dust coating induces a grooming sequence in Drosophila (eyes > antennae > abdomen > wings > notum) through hierarchical suppression, but it remained unconfirmed whether simultaneous activation of sensory neurons across the body would elicit the same prioritized response.
evaluation: Claims C11-C18 accurately describe prior work (Seeds et al., 2014) and identify the knowledge gap addressed by the current study. C18 explicitly acknowledges what was not previously confirmed, providing clear motivation for the experiments. The claims are appropriately supported by citations and logical inference.

result: Three GAL4 lines (R52A06-, R30B01-, and R81E10-GAL4) were identified that express in sensory neurons across the body, predominantly mechanosensory neurons, and optogenetic activation of these neurons elicits site-directed grooming responses.
evaluation: Claims C19-C25 are supported by confocal microscopy data (Figure 1A-G) and optogenetic experiments (Figure 1H, Videos 1-2). The anatomical characterization is based on established classification criteria (citations provided), and the behavioral responses are demonstrated experimentally. Statistical analysis (Chi-squared test, p<0.0001) supports the site-directed grooming claims.

result: Simultaneous optogenetic activation of sensory neurons across the body elicits head grooming preferentially, followed by posterior body grooming after stimulus cessation, demonstrating hierarchical suppression and persistent neural activity that maintains the grooming sequence.
evaluation: Claims C26-C33 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-B and supplementary figures. The decapitation control (C28) effectively rules out a delay explanation (C29), supporting the suppression hypothesis (C30). The continuation of grooming after stimulus cessation (C32) provides evidence for persistent neural activity (C33). The experimental design is rigorous with appropriate controls.

result: Reactivation of sensory neurons during posterior grooming causes flies to terminate posterior grooming and switch to head grooming, providing optogenetic evidence consistent with hierarchical suppression.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by data in Figure 2A and supplementary figures. The termination of posterior grooming upon reactivation (C34-C35) is quantitatively demonstrated, and the effect persists even with shortened intervals (C36). This provides direct evidence for the hierarchical suppression mechanism, strengthening conclusions from dust-based experiments.

result: Interommatidial bristle mechanosensory neurons on Drosophila eyes, identified using VT17251-LexA, project to the subesophageal zone (SEZ) and elicit eye grooming when optogenetically activated.
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by anatomical data (Figure 3A-B) and behavioral experiments (Figure 3C). The identification is based on homology with other insects (citations provided) and confirmed by expression pattern analysis. The optogenetic activation demonstrates functional relevance. The comparative anatomy (C41) adds valuable context.

result: The spGAL4 line R30B01-AD ∩ R31H10-DBD was generated to restrict expression to wing and haltere sensory neurons, including campaniform sensilla and mechanosensory bristle neurons, which project to the VNS with some ascending to the SEZ.
evaluation: Claims C43-C53 are supported by detailed anatomical characterization (Figure 4A-F) with quantitative neuron counts. The use of Split GAL4 technique (C45) is appropriately cited and addresses the limitation identified in C44. The anatomical descriptions are precise with median values reported. The inference about projection patterns (C53) is appropriately qualified and supported by citations.

result: Optogenetic activation of neurons targeted by R30B01-AD ∩ R31H10-DBD elicited wing but not haltere grooming, most parsimoniously explained by activation of wing sensory neurons, though haltere involvement cannot be ruled out.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 4G). The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitation (C56) that haltere campaniform sensilla expression prevents definitive conclusions about which neurons drive the behavior. This honest assessment of uncertainty is scientifically appropriate, though it slightly weakens the specificity of the result.

result: Individual activation of eye bristle mechanosensory neurons or wing/haltere sensory neurons elicits only their corresponding grooming movements (eye or wing grooming respectively) without triggering other movements or sequences.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by experimental data (Figure 5A, Videos 6-7). The specificity of responses (C59-C60) is important for establishing that the sequence requires simultaneous activation. The differential persistence (C57 vs C58) provides additional mechanistic insight. The data clearly demonstrate the claimed specificity.

result: Simultaneous optogenetic activation of eye and wing/haltere sensory neurons using R31H10-AD ∩ R34E03-DBD elicits prioritized grooming starting with eyes then proceeding to wings, with eye grooming suppressing wing grooming, demonstrating hierarchical suppression through direct sensory neuron activation.
evaluation: Claims C61-C67 are supported by anatomical (Figure 5B) and behavioral data (Figure 5A, supplementary figures, Video 8). The prioritization is clearly demonstrated (C62, C65). The transition during stimulation (C63) is interesting but C64 appropriately notes this is speculative. The conclusion (C66-C67) is well-supported and represents a key finding confirming the parallel activation model.

result: Bristle mechanosensory neurons can elicit grooming, though the hypothesis that bristle numbers determine suppression hierarchy receives mixed support from bristle counts across body parts.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by the experimental data. C69-C70 are appropriately cited prior work. However, C71-C73 present an analysis of bristle numbers that yields contradictory results: eyes have more bristles than wings (consistent with hierarchy) but notum has more than wings (inconsistent). The authors appropriately note this argues against the hypothesis, but the analysis is incomplete and doesn't account for other sensory neuron types mentioned. This weakens but doesn't invalidate the overall findings.

result: Neural circuits controlling Drosophila grooming movements have mechanisms for maintaining excitability, as evidenced by persistent grooming that continues beyond optogenetic activation, a feature also observed in vertebrates.
evaluation: Claims C74-C81 integrate prior work (C74-C76, C78, C80) with current findings (C77, C79). The persistence of wing grooming (C79) is demonstrated in the current study (Figure 5A). The comparison to vertebrates (C80) and speculation about function (C81) are appropriately qualified. The synthesis of evidence across species strengthens the conclusion about persistent excitability mechanisms.

result: Flies maintain a persistent trace of stimulated body parts that allows delayed sequential grooming, occurring through parallel activation of grooming movements where later movements remain active without further sensory input and are elicited once suppression from earlier movements ceases.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85, C87, C91 present a mechanistic model supported by the observation that grooming continues after stimulus cessation (demonstrated in multiple figures). The postulated mechanism (C83-C85) is a reasonable inference from the data, though direct neural recordings would strengthen it. The connection to temporal summation (C87) provides additional theoretical support. The model revision (C91) appropriately updates prior work based on new observations.

result: Previous computational models indicated constant stimulation was necessary for grooming movements, and such models describe grooming well over long time scales (~30 min).
evaluation: Claims C86, C88-C90 describe prior modeling work (Seeds et al., 2014) and are appropriately cited. These claims provide context for the current findings and explain how the new observations (persistent activity on shorter time scales) extend rather than contradict the previous model. The distinction between time scales is important for understanding the complete system.

result: The study employed appropriate transgenic lines, optogenetic methods, and anatomical classification approaches, with methodological decisions justified by the properties of the optogenetic tools and experimental observations.
evaluation: Claims C92-C102 describe methodological details that are appropriately documented and justified. The choice of ChR2 vs CsChrimson (C96, C98) is well-reasoned based on light penetration properties. The optimization of light power (C99-C100) demonstrates careful experimental design. The classification methods (C101-C102) are based on established criteria with appropriate citations. These methodological claims are well-supported.
